evals.prompt: We have a second-generation FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system (fs-0gen2prod12345678, DeploymentType=MULTI_AZ_2, ThroughputCapacity=4096 MBps, DiskIopsConfiguration={Mode: USER_PROVISIONED, Iops: 80000}) in us-east-1. Over the trailing 7-day window, CloudWatch returned no datapoints for StorageCapacityUtilization, while detailed per-tier metrics returned StorageUsed{StorageTier=SSD,DataType=All}=1,979,120,929,996 bytes (~1.80 TiB) and StorageCapacity{StorageTier=SSD,DataType=All}=2,147,483,648,000 bytes (~1.95 TiB). Meanwhile, p95 FileServerDiskIopsUtilization is 93.4% and p95 DiskIopsUtilization is 41.2%, with p95 CPUUtilization at 68%. How should these performance metrics be evaluated and remediated?
evals.expected_output: Explains that Gen2 (MULTI_AZ_2) file systems do not emit StorageCapacityUtilization (not 0%), computes SSD utilization via StorageUsed{SSD} / StorageCapacity{SSD} (~92.16%), flags PERF-05 as Critical (>90% where tiering promotion stops), and distinguishes FileServerDiskIopsUtilization (93.4% Fail — throughput-capacity tier / HA-pair limit) from DiskIopsUtilization (41.2% — provisioned SSD IOPS not the bottleneck).
expectations: Explains that second-generation FSxN file systems (DeploymentType ending in _2 such as MULTI_AZ_2) do not emit StorageCapacityUtilization, so missing datapoints must not be treated as 0% and must fall back to StorageUsed{SSD} divided by StorageCapacity{SSD}
Computes SSD utilization at ~92.2% (above 90%) and flags PERF-05 as Critical because tiering promotion stops above 90% SSD utilization (leaving hot data in the capacity pool at 15-25 ms latency)

Identifies p95 FileServerDiskIopsUtilization (93.4% > 90%) as the saturated constraint rather than DiskIopsUtilization (41.2%), recommending throughput-capacity tier / HA-pair scaling (and checking 4 KB write amplification) rather than raising provisioned SSD IOPS
Marks PERF-01 (sustained p95 CPUUtilization at 68% < 85%) as Pass

evals.prompt:
During an FSx for NetApp ONTAP audit of fs-0prodontap9999999 (SVM svm-0111222333, Name=svm_erp), fsx:DescribeVolumes returned three volumes:
1. fsvol-0root0000001 (Name=svm_erp_root, OntapVolumeType=RW, JunctionPath='/', SizeInMegabytes=1024, SnapshotPolicy=default, StorageEfficiencyEnabled=true) with StorageUsed=20,971,520 bytes and 0 DataReadOperations/DataWriteOperations.
2. fsvol-0dpdr0000002 (Name=erp_dr_mirror, OntapVolumeType=DP, SizeInMegabytes=524288, SnapshotPolicy=none, StorageEfficiencyEnabled=true) with 0 DataReadOperations/DataWriteOperations.
3. fsvol-0appdata0003 (Name=erp_prod_db, OntapVolumeType=RW, JunctionPath='/erp_db', SizeInMegabytes=1048576, SnapshotPolicy=none, StorageEfficiencyEnabled=false) with StorageUsed=966,367,641,600 bytes and 0 DataReadOperations/DataWriteOperations over the trailing window.

expectations: Excludes the SVM root volume fsvol-0root0000001 (JunctionPath='/') ONLY in OPS-10 ('Excluded — SVM root') while tagging it in other checks and explicitly never recommending deleting/removing it

Treats fsvol-0dpdr0000002 (OntapVolumeType=DP SnapMirror destination) as Informational in OPS-02 and BKP-03 — never flagging it for removal or failing BKP-03, while noting SnapMirror lag/health is not exposed by public AWS APIs

Flags RW data volume fsvol-0appdata0003 for OPS-06 (High — SnapshotPolicy='none'), OPS-05 (Medium — StorageEfficiencyEnabled=false), OPS-02 (Medium — zero I/O on RW data volume), and OPS-10 (~88% used = 966,367,641,600 / (1,048,576 * 1024 * 1024), Warning 80-90%)
Marks OPS-11 (aged snapshots) as 'Not evaluated — not available via public API' rather than Pass, explaining fsx:DescribeSnapshots does not return ONTAP snapshots

evals.prompt:
Help us interpret CloudWatch metrics from two FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems:
- On fs-0active1111111111, RW volume fsvol-0hotvol999 has TieringPolicy=ALL. Over the 7-day window (168 hours), CapacityPoolReadBytes summed to 3,248,742,072,320 bytes (~3,025.6 GiB / ~18.0 GiB/hr), DataReadOperationTime summed to 2,150 seconds across 100,000 DataReadOperations, and DataWriteOperationTime summed to 180 seconds across 150,000 DataWriteOperations.
- On fs-0idle222222222222 (a newly provisioned pre-prod file system with no client mounts yet), DataReadOperationTime, DataReadOperations, and FileServerCacheHitRatio returned zero datapoints.
How should latency, cache hit ratio, and capacity-pool tiering be scored across both file systems?
evals.expected_output: Converts seconds-based OperationTime / Operations into milliseconds (21.5 ms read latency, 1.2 ms write latency), flags Critical PERF-17 and High PERF-21 on fsvol-0hotvol999 because ALL tiering on an active RW volume is serving ~18 GB/hr from the capacity pool at 15-25 ms latency (remediate to AUTO or NONE), and marks latency/cache checks on idle fs-0idle222222222222 as 'Not evaluated' rather than 0% or Pass.
expectations: Computes read latency as DataReadOperationTime / DataReadOperations * 1000 = 21.5 ms and write latency as 180 / 150,000 * 1000 = 1.2 ms, explicitly converting seconds to milliseconds (ms)

Flags Critical PERF-17 and High PERF-21 (Fail, > 10 GB/hr) because RW volume fsvol-0hotvol999 uses TieringPolicy=ALL with active CapacityPoolReadBytes (~18 GB/hr), causing 15-25 ms capacity-pool read latency, and recommends changing tiering to AUTO or NONE

Marks activity-dependent checks (PERF-22 cache hit ratio and PERF-23 latency) on idle fs-0idle222222222222 with no datapoints as 'Not evaluated' (stating the reason) — never guessing 0% or reporting a false Pass

evals.prompt: Audit the security posture of FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system fs-0sec8888888888888 (DeploymentType=MULTI_AZ_1, KmsKeyId=arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:123456789012:key/aws-managed-fsx-default, RouteTableIds=[rtb-0aaa111], NetworkInterfaceIds=[eni-0111, eni-0222]). Our SVM svm-0smbonly has ActiveDirectoryConfiguration set, volume fsvol-01 has SecurityStyle=NTFS, and volume fsvol-02 has SecurityStyle=MIXED. Resolving eni-0111 and eni-0222 shows security group sg-0fsxopen, which allows inbound TCP 445 from 0.0.0.0/0 (no NFS ports 2049/111/635/4045-4046 are open) and outbound all-protocols (-1) to 0.0.0.0/0. Meanwhile, route table rtb-0aaa111 is missing routes for the file system's EndpointIpAddressRange. What findings should be reported?
evals.expected_output: Explains ENI-based SG resolution, recognizes SMB/CIFS protocol in use (TCP 445 open, so missing NFS ports are NOT flagged in SEC-01), flags Critical SEC-02 (0.0.0.0/0 inbound), Warning SEC-04 (MIXED security style on fsvol-02), Fail SEC-06 (missing Multi-AZ floating-IP route in rtb-0aaa111), Informational/Medium SEC-07 (always encrypted at rest; AWS-managed key vs CMK immutability requiring migration), and Fail SEC-08 (0.0.0.0/0 all-protocols egress).
expectations: Confirms security groups are resolved via NetworkInterfaceIds -> DescribeNetworkInterfaces -> SecurityGroups, and evaluates SEC-01 protocol-aware for SMB/CIFS (port 445) without falsely requiring NFS ports (2049/111/635/4045-4046) on an SMB-only SVM
Flags SEC-02 as Critical Fail for inbound 0.0.0.0/0 on sg-0fsxopen and SEC-08 as Medium Fail for 0.0.0.0/0 all-protocols (-1) egress
Flags SEC-04 Warning for SecurityStyle=MIXED on fsvol-02 and SEC-06 Medium Fail for missing Multi-AZ floating-IP route in rtb-0aaa111

Reports SEC-07 accurately: notes FSx for NetApp ONTAP is always encrypted at rest (never 'unencrypted'), distinguishes AWS-managed KMS key vs CMK, and states KMS keys cannot be changed in place after creation

evals.prompt: Our storage team runs a first-generation single-HA-pair FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system (DeploymentType=MULTI_AZ_1, HAPairs=1) for a write-heavy database workload. They doubled ThroughputCapacity from 1,024 MBps to 2,048 MBps, yet sustained SSD write throughput is still hitting a hard wall right around 1,024 MBps. Why didn't raising the throughput tier increase SSD write throughput, and what architecture change is required?
evals.expected_output: Explains PERF-18 and PERF-16: each HA pair has a 1,024 MBps SSD write ceiling that cannot be raised by increasing ThroughputCapacity alone on a single-HA-pair file system, and scaling past that ceiling requires multiple scale-out HA pairs on a second-generation FSx for ONTAP file system (MULTI_AZ_2 / SINGLE_AZ_2 — note MULTI_AZ_2 vs SINGLE_AZ_2 HA pair support).
expectations: Identifies the ~1,024 MBps per-HA-pair SSD write ceiling (PERF-18) and explains why increasing ThroughputCapacity to 2,048 MBps on a single-HA-pair (HAPairs=1) file system cannot raise single-HA-pair SSD write throughput

Explains the generation / HA-pair remediation (PERF-16 / PERF-18): moving to a second-generation FSx for NetApp ONTAP deployment with multiple HA pairs (or distributing writes across HA pairs / file systems) rather than only raising throughput tier

evals.prompt: Before we migrate compliance archives onto FSx for NetApp ONTAP, what is the exact difference between SnapLock Enterprise and SnapLock Compliance volumes on FSx for NetApp ONTAP — specifically regarding whether a volume or locked WORM file can ever be deleted by an administrator (or by deleting the AWS FSx file system) before its retention period expires?
evals.expected_output: Queries AWS documentation via awsknowledge or aws-mcp documentation tools (1-2 focused lookups) without raw CLI commands, and accurately contrasts SnapLock Enterprise (allows privileged deletion of SnapLock Enterprise volumes by authorized admins) with SnapLock Compliance (strict regulatory WORM — neither locked files nor the volume/file system can be deleted before retention expires, even by root/fsxadmin or AWS account admins).
expectations: Uses awsknowledge or aws-mcp documentation search/read tools to verify official FSx for NetApp ONTAP SnapLock documentation and executes zero raw aws CLI shell commands

Accurately explains that SnapLock Compliance enforces strict irreversible WORM retention where locked files, the SnapLock Compliance volume, and the parent FSx file system cannot be deleted until retention periods expire

Contrasts SnapLock Enterprise, where a privileged administrator can delete a SnapLock Enterprise volume (though individual locked files remain protected against normal modification/deletion during retention)
